label: Isoperimetric-type Inequalities
notes: This chapter, printed pages 545 through 566, asks how much boundary a region must carry once its volume is fixed. We organize the answer through curvature-dimension and transport. The slogan is that lower Ricci bounds force regions to behave at least as well as their counterparts in a fixed model space.

label: The Classical Isoperimetric Problem
notes: Among all regions of a given volume, which one minimizes boundary measure? In Euclidean space the ball wins, and the inequality controls the boundary-to-volume ratio. We restate it through the isoperimetric profile so that the same question can be transported to any metric-measure space with a curvature floor.

label: The Isoperimetric Profile
notes: The isoperimetric profile records, for each fraction of total volume, the smallest possible perimeter of a region of that size. Reading the profile is the whole game: a higher profile means the space separates volume more cheaply, and comparison theorems bound it from below by a model profile.

label: Curvature-Dimension CD(K,N)
notes: The curvature-dimension condition packages a lower Ricci bound K and an upper dimension bound N into displacement convexity of entropy along Wasserstein geodesics. This synthetic formulation needs no smooth structure, so it travels to singular spaces while still forcing the geometric concentration that isoperimetry detects.

label: The Model Space
notes: Every comparison needs a reference. For CD(K,N) the model is the one-dimensional weighted line whose density realizes the extreme curvature-dimension parameters, such as a sphere of the right radius when K is positive. Its isoperimetric profile is computed once and becomes the universal benchmark.

label: Levy-Gromov Inequality
notes: Levy-Gromov states that on a manifold with Ricci at least K and dimension N, any region's boundary measure is at least that of a spherical cap enclosing the same volume fraction in the model sphere. Curvature alone, not the detailed shape, sets the floor on perimeter.

label: Transport Map Construction
notes: The transport proof pushes the model measure onto the target measure with the Brenier-McCann optimal map. The map is the gradient of a convex potential, and its Jacobian carries volume distortion. Restricting the map to a region and tracking the boundary turns a measure comparison into a perimeter comparison.

label: Jacobian and Volume Distortion
notes: Along the transport interpolation the Jacobian determinant obeys a concavity governed by Ricci curvature through the Bochner formula. Lower curvature bounds the determinant's growth, so a region cannot shrink its boundary faster than the model allows. This pointwise inequality is the analytic engine of the comparison.

label: Isoperimetric Comparison
notes: Putting it together: fix a volume fraction, transport the model region of that size, and the curvature-controlled Jacobian guarantees the image carries at least the model perimeter. The picture contrasts a wiggly large-perimeter region with the smooth model region of equal area and smaller boundary.

label: Functional Form and Deficit
notes: Isoperimetry has a softened functional twin: Gaussian and exponential concentration, and a sharp deficit measuring distance from the extremal ball. The deficit vanishes exactly at the model region, and stability theorems control how a near-optimal region must resemble that ball up to small error.

label: Consequences for Ric >= K
notes: A spectral gap, diameter bounds, and concentration of measure all follow once the isoperimetric profile is pinned below by the model. Spaces with Ricci at least K thus inherit a coherent package of geometric and analytic controls, even when only the synthetic curvature-dimension condition is available.

label: Summary and Outlook
notes: We connected fixed volume, minimal boundary, curvature floors, and transport maps into one comparison principle. Levy-Gromov is its sharpest classical instance, and the synthetic CD(K,N) version extends it to metric-measure spaces. Next chapters use these isoperimetric controls to study concentration and the geometry of limit spaces.
